claims.text: The investigated material consists of sub-5 nm AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles made by pulsed laser deposition on a silicon nitride membrane.
The as-grown AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles initially have an FCC structure and elliptical, icosahedral, or truncated-octahedral geometries.
Surface-energy gradients make atomic diffusion active in AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
Au and Cu preferentially segregate to the nanoparticle surface.
Surface-energy-driven diffusion overrides the sluggish-diffusion effect expected from bulk high-entropy-alloy thermodynamics.
In sub-5 nm particles, a high surface-to-volume ratio causes surface-energy minimization to dominate configurational-entropy stabilization.
The proposed surface-driven mechanism becomes dominant at approximately 600–800 K.
Below the proposed 600–800 K threshold, the FCC structure is kinetically trapped.
Above the proposed threshold, surface diffusion accelerates and changes particle shape from elliptical to spherical.
Accelerated surface diffusion causes coalescence, loss of sub-5 nm particles, and widening of the particle-size distribution.
Au and Cu are low-surface-energy elements whose surface segregation leads to their evaporation.
Icosahedral nanoparticles have greater surface strain than truncated-octahedral nanoparticles.
Icosahedral nanoparticles segregate and evaporate more rapidly than truncated octahedra because of their greater surface strain.
The mechanism is dominant in sub-10 nm nanoparticles and becomes less relevant in larger particles or bulk material.
High-entropy alloys are commonly associated with sluggish atomic diffusion and high microstructural stability.
High entropy and sluggish diffusion stabilize FCC AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles specifically against segregation and coalescence.
The exact onset temperature depends on particle size, substrate interaction, and initial defect density.

The proposed test compares AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles having identical bulk composition but different controlled surface terminations at temperatures above and below 600–800 K using in situ STEM and atomistic simulations.
If surface-energy gradients alone cause phase separation, atomistic simulations omitting a sluggish-diffusion assumption should reproduce the observed segregation and evaporation.
Failure of such simulations to reproduce the observations would indicate that additional kinetic or thermodynamic factors are required.
